name: cigar
title: Cigar — Patience Made Smoke
essence: A cigar is the arbitrage between leaf and fire. Patience made smoke.

story.title: From Seed to Smoke — the zero to one of the cigar
story.essence: A cigar is a plant taught to burn slowly. The gap between a green leaf and a gray ash is five years wide. Everything in between is the craft.

chapters.title: Before the name
chapters.story: Tobacco is American. For thousands of years the peoples of the Caribbean and Mesoamerica grew it, dried it, and burned it as ritual — a carved relief at Palenque shows a Maya figure drawing smoke from a rolled tube. The Taíno of Cuba called their rolled leaves by a word the world would inherit: cohiba. Smoke was not leisure. It was prayer made visible.

chapters.title: First contact
chapters.story: In November 1492, on Cuba, two of Columbus's crew — Rodrigo de Jerez and Luis de Torres — watched Taíno people drink smoke from burning rolls of leaf. Jerez carried the habit home to Spain, and the story goes the Inquisition jailed him for it: only the devil, they reasoned, gives a man the power to exhale smoke. Two worlds met in a single breath. The cigar was the bridge.

chapters.title: Seville and smoke
chapters.story: Spain made tobacco a crown monopoly and funneled Cuban leaf through Seville, where the great Royal Tobacco Factory rose in the eighteenth century — later the setting of Bizet's Carmen. Around 1560 the French diplomat Jean Nicot sent leaf to the court of France; nicotine still carries his name. Europe learned to smoke before it learned why.

chapters.title: Havana rises
chapters.story: In 1817 a royal decree ended the monopoly, and Cuba was free to roll and sell its own. The great houses followed: H. Upmann in 1844, Partagás in 1845, Hoyo de Monterrey in 1865, Romeo y Julieta in 1875. From 1865, lectores read novels and news aloud to the rollers at their benches — Dumas was a favorite, and one factory's cigars took the name Montecristo. The golden age of Havana was a factory full of listening hands.

chapters.title: Exile and embargo
chapters.story: The revolution of 1959 nationalized the factories, and in 1962 the United States embargoed the island — though President Kennedy first sent Pierre Salinger to gather some 1,200 H. Upmann petit coronas the night before he signed. The great families scattered: to the Dominican Republic, to Honduras, to Nicaragua, to the Canary Islands, carrying seed and memory. The gap between homeland and craft opened wide. The exiles rolled across it.

chapters.title: The new world answers
chapters.story: In exile the craft took new root: Padrón in Miami from 1964, Joya de Nicaragua in Estelí from 1968, the Fuentes rebuilding in the Dominican Republic. The boom of the 1990s — Cigar Aficionado launched in 1992 — remade the industry, and in 1995 Fuente Fuente OpusX proved a great wrapper could grow in Dominican soil. Cuba was no longer the only answer. It became one answer among several true ones.

chapters.title: The leaf now
chapters.story: Nicaragua's volcanic valleys now stand beside Vuelta Abajo in the reckoning of the world's best leaf, and small factories treat blending the way winemakers treat vineyards. A cigar still cannot be hurried: seed to smoke remains a matter of years. In an accelerating world, the cigar is a deliberate slowness. The leaf is.

regions.name: Vuelta Abajo
regions.known_for: The most celebrated tobacco land on earth — wrapper, binder, and filler for habanos
regions.note: A small zone of Pinar del Río around San Juan y Martínez and San Luis, where red sand and soft climate grow every leaf a Cuban cigar needs.

regions.name: Partido
regions.note: Close to Havana, its fields tented in cloth; the fine, elastic wrappers of the classic habano are grown here.

regions.name: Cibao Valley
regions.known_for: The heart of one of the world's largest premium-cigar industries
regions.note: Around Santiago de los Caballeros, exile houses rebuilt after 1959; for decades more premium cigars shipped from here than anywhere else, and it still vies with Nicaragua for that crown.

regions.name: Estelí
regions.known_for: Dark, powerful ligero from black volcanic soil
regions.note: The engine of the modern full-bodied cigar; strength with a pepper edge that blenders reach for when they want thunder.

regions.name: Jalapa Valley
regions.note: Estelí's counterweight — the same country, a gentler soil; blenders marry the two the way a chef balances heat and sugar.

regions.name: Danlí and the Jamastrán Valley
regions.known_for: Rich, earthy leaf and a deep factory tradition
regions.note: Honduras's cigar capital, settled by Cuban exiles; its tobacco carries weight and a dry, woody depth.

regions.name: San Andrés Valley
regions.note: In Veracruz, a native leaf that ferments dark and sweet — the chocolate-and-earth wrapper behind many of the great modern maduros.

regions.name: Connecticut River Valley
regions.known_for: Connecticut Shade wrapper and Connecticut Broadleaf
regions.note: Under cloth tents grows the pale, silky shade wrapper; in open sun grows the thick broadleaf that becomes classic maduro.

regions.name: Ecuador
regions.note: A permanent high overcast does the work of shade tents; Ecuadorian Connecticut and Habano wrappers now dress cigars worldwide.

regions.name: Bahia
regions.known_for: Mata Fina and Mata Norte — dark, naturally sweet leaf
regions.note: Brazilian sun-grown tobacco ferments into some of the sweetest maduro character in the blender's palette.

brands.name: Cohiba
brands.style: Medium to full — grassy, honeyed, unmistakably Cuban
brands.why: Born at the El Laguito factory as Fidel Castro's private and diplomatic cigar, unavailable to the public until 1982. Its seco and ligero take a rare extra fermentation in barrels — patience layered on patience, and it carries the Taíno word for tobacco itself.

brands.name: Montecristo
brands.style: Medium — tangy cocoa and wood, the benchmark habano
brands.why: Named for the Dumas novel the lectores read aloud to the rollers, it became the best-selling habano in the world. The Montecristo No. 4 is the cigar by which countless smokers learned what Cuba tastes like.

brands.name: Partagás
brands.why: Don Jaime Partagás built his factory in the heart of Havana, and the house has stood for the dark, powerful end of the Cuban spectrum ever since. Few names say 'old Havana' with more authority.

brands.name: H. Upmann
brands.style: Light to medium — refined, woody, composed
brands.why: Founded by Herman Upmann, a German banker who loved cigars enough to move to Havana for them. Its petit coronas were the ones President Kennedy secured the night before signing the embargo — elegance certified at the highest level.

brands.name: Romeo y Julieta
brands.style: Medium — aromatic, balanced, romantic by name and nature
brands.why: Winston Churchill smoked them so devotedly that the marque named its 7 x 47 vitola after him, and the Churchill became a size the whole industry uses. A love story from Verona, retold in leaf.

brands.name: Hoyo de Monterrey
brands.style: Light to medium — delicate, creamy, morning-bright
brands.why: José Gener named it for the gate of his Vuelta Abajo plantation — the 'hollow' of Monterrey, a low river-fed field of superb wrapper. It is the proof that a Cuban cigar can whisper and still be heard.

brands.name: Trinidad
brands.style: Medium — spicy cream, rolled in small numbers
brands.why: For decades it existed only as a gift of the Cuban state, handed to diplomats and never sold; the public could not buy one until 1998. Scarcity was its first fame, but the cigar kept the reputation the mystery began.

brands.name: Davidoff
brands.style: Mild to medium — immaculate construction, quiet complexity
brands.why: Zino Davidoff, the great Geneva tobacconist, turned retail into philosophy and helped teach the world to store cigars in humidors. The brand was rolled in Cuba until 1990, then remade itself in the Dominican Republic without losing its polish.

brands.name: Arturo Fuente
brands.style: Mild to full across lines — Dominican mastery, Cameroon sweetness
brands.why: Founded in Tampa by a Cuban emigrant and rebuilt through fires and exile by four generations of one family. In 1995 the Fuente Fuente OpusX proved a world-class wrapper could be grown in Dominican soil — a thing the industry had called impossible.

brands.name: Padrón
brands.style: Full — cocoa, coffee, and box-pressed depth
brands.why: José Orlando Padrón left Cuba, started in Miami with a few hundred saved dollars and one roller, and bet everything on Nicaraguan sun-grown leaf. The 1964 Anniversary Series set the standard by which modern full-bodied cigars are judged.

brands.name: Joya de Nicaragua
brands.style: Medium to full — rustic strength with volcanic spice
brands.why: Nicaragua's first premium cigar factory, standing in Estelí through revolution and war. Every Nicaraguan cigar made since owes something to the door this house opened.

brands.name: Drew Estate
brands.style: Experimental to full — from infused ACID to the dark Liga Privada
brands.why: Jonathan Drew went to Estelí with almost nothing and built one of the largest factories in Nicaragua on a single idea: the cigar was not finished evolving. The traditionalists frowned, then quietly took notes.

collections.name: The Havana Founders
collections.essence: The nineteenth-century houses that made Havana the capital of smoke. The names on these bands are older than most nations' constitutions.

collections.name: The Diplomatic Pouch
collections.essence: Cigars born as instruments of state — rolled for presidents and gifted to the world before the world was allowed to buy them.

collections.name: The Exiles
collections.essence: Cuban-born families who lost the island and kept the craft. The gap between homeland and memory — they rolled across it.

collections.name: The Nicaraguan Wave
collections.essence: Black volcanic soil, sun-hardened ligero, and the factories of Estelí — the new world's answer to Vuelta Abajo.

collections.name: The Gentle Door
collections.essence: Where to begin: composed, mild-to-medium cigars that reward attention without demanding endurance.

collections.name: The Long Night
collections.essence: Full-bodied, slow-burning cigars for the unhurried hour after dinner — strength with something to say.

stores.name: James J. Fox
stores.note: Cigars have been sold on this site since 1787, when it traded as Robert Lewis. Winston Churchill's ledger and his favorite chair are still kept in the shop's small museum.

stores.name: Davidoff of Geneva
stores.note: The Davidoff family shop where Zino Davidoff grew up among the leaves and later taught the world that a cigar deserves a humidor. Retail as scholarship.

stores.name: La Casa del Habano
stores.note: The official franchise network of Habanos S.A. — the sanctioned houses of the Cuban cigar, with walk-in humidors and rolling demonstrations from Havana outward.

stores.name: The Partagás shop, Havana
stores.note: The store attached to the old Real Fábrica de Tabacos Partagás, behind the Capitolio — a pilgrimage site where the smoke of the nineteenth century still seems to hang.

stores.name: Casa Fuente
stores.note: The Fuente family's lounge and shop in the Forum Shops at Caesars Palace — the rare place built by the growers themselves, OpusX behind glass.

stores.name: Iwan Ries & Co.
stores.note: A family tobacco house trading since 1857 — one of the oldest in America, five generations deep.

stores.name: Nat Sherman Townhouse
stores.note: Founded in 1930, its 42nd Street Townhouse was New York's cathedral of tobacco until it closed in 2020. Gone, and still named with reverence.

process.essence: From a seed smaller than a grain of sand to a finished cigar is a matter of years. Nothing in the chain can be rushed; every stage is a form of waiting done correctly.

stages.title: The seedbed
stages.what: Tobacco seeds — thousands fit in a spoon — are germinated in protected seedbeds and trays for about 45 days until the seedlings can stand the field.
stages.why: Everything the cigar will become is already in this dust. The grower's first job is simply to keep the future alive.

stages.title: The field
stages.what: Seedlings are transplanted and grown for two to three months — in full sun for filler and dark wrapper, or under cloth tents (tapado) for fine shade wrapper.
stages.why: Sun thickens the leaf and loads it with oils and strength; shade keeps it thin, elastic, and even. The light decides the leaf's destiny.

stages.title: The priming
stages.what: Leaves are picked by hand, two or three at a time, from the bottom of the plant upward as each level ripens — volado low, seco in the middle, ligero at the top.
stages.why: Position is character: the highest leaves take the most sun and carry the most power. A plant is harvested the way a story is read — in order.

stages.title: The curing barn
stages.what: Leaves are sewn in pairs and hung on poles in the casa de tabaco, air-curing for 45 to 60 days as green turns gold, then brown.
stages.why: Curing removes water and chlorophyll. The leaf dies slowly and deliberately, which is the only way it can be useful.

stages.title: The pilón
stages.what: Cured leaves are moistened and stacked into pilones — dense piles that heat themselves from within — then torn down, turned, and rebuilt, again and again over months.
stages.why: Fermentation is what makes tobacco smokable: harshness and ammonia leave, aroma arrives. This is the cigar's true birth.

stages.title: The sleep
stages.what: Fermented leaf is baled — traditionally in palm-bark tercios — and rested in aging rooms for months or years before anyone rolls it.
stages.why: Time rounds what fire and heat began. Great factories sit on warehouses of sleeping leaf the way banks sit on gold.

stages.title: The despalillo
stages.what: Workers strip the central stem from each leaf and grade the leaf by size, color, and texture — wrapper apart from binder, binder apart from filler.
stages.why: A cigar is built from chosen leaves, not available ones. Sorting is where standards become physical.

stages.title: The blend
stages.what: The master blender writes the recipe: how much ligero for strength, seco for aroma, volado for an even burn, and which binder and wrapper complete it.
stages.why: No single leaf is a cigar. The blend is the composition — the difference between noise and music.

stages.title: The torcedor
stages.what: At the bench, filler is bunched into the binder, pressed in molds, then dressed in the wrapper and finished — in the Cuban manner — with a triple cap.
stages.why: Years of agriculture pass through two human hands in a few minutes. The roller is where the leaf becomes the object.

stages.title: The marriage
stages.what: Finished cigars rest in the escaparate — the cool cedar aging room — until their moistures equalize and the blend settles; then they are color-sorted, banded, and boxed.
stages.why: A just-rolled cigar is an argument still in progress. Rest lets the leaves agree with each other before the fire asks its question.

fermentation.essence: Fermentation is the arbitrage between a cured leaf and a smokable one. The pile heats itself, the harshness leaves as ammonia, and what remains is aroma. Without it, tobacco is just a dry plant.
fermentation.science: Cured leaves are moistened and stacked into pilones — piles whose own weight and moisture ignite enzymatic and microbial activity. The core temperature climbs to roughly 100–140°F as ammonia and other impurities are driven off, nicotine softens, and the leaf's sugars and acids are transformed. Before the pile overheats, workers tear it down, rotate the leaves from outside to center, and rebuild it — over and over, for weeks at a time. Most leaf ferments at least twice; thick, dark leaf destined for maduro ferments longer and hotter. It is composting steered just short of destruction, and it is what makes tobacco smokable.
vessels: Casa de tabaco — the air-curing barn where the leaf first browns
Pilón — the self-heating fermentation pile, the cigar's true crucible
Tercio — the palm-bark bale in which fermented leaf sleeps
Cedar-lined aging rooms, where time finishes what heat began
Oak barrels — used for rare extra fermentations of the finest leaf
Escaparate — the cool room where finished cigars marry before boxing
notes: Push a hand into a working pilón and it is hot — the leaf burning without fire.
The smell of ammonia leaving the pile is the smell of harshness departing.
Turn the pilón or lose it: an unturned pile overheats and cooks the crop.
Maduro is not a dye but a duration — darker because it fermented longer.
Curing dries the leaf. Fermentation civilizes it.

selection.essence: Choosing a cigar is reading a leaf before the fire does. Look, touch, and be honest about the hour you have.

guide.how: Look for even color, a faint oily sheen, and fine veins — no cracks, tears, or dry patches. The wrapper is a large share of the flavor and all of the first impression.
Pinch gently along the body: it should give evenly, with no soft voids or hard knots. A well-made cigar feels consistent from foot to head.
A good draw pulls like sipping through a straw — neither a fight nor a free fall. Too tight will not smoke; too loose will burn hot and fast.
A robusto asks about 45 minutes; a Churchill wants ninety or more. Choose the cigar to fit the time you actually have — a rushed cigar is a wasted one.
Strength is nicotine; body is the weight of flavor; they are not the same. Start mild-to-medium and climb as your palate learns the map.
Keep cigars in a humidor at 65–70% relative humidity and around 65–70°F. Too dry, it burns hot and bitter; too wet, it draws badly and risks mold. A cigar is alive until it is lit.
Buy from reputable merchants. Counterfeit Cubans are an industry of their own; provenance is part of the purchase.
A cigar that has just traveled is out of balance. Let it rest in your humidor for a few weeks before lighting — the blend re-settles, and the cigar you smoke is the one the blender intended.

rituals.essence: A ritual is the arbitrage between burning a cigar and smoking one. The cigar is slow on purpose; the ceremony is the point.

rites.name: The inspection and the cold draw
rites.how: Before any flame, look the wrapper over and pinch gently along the body for soft spots or hard knots. Then cut, and draw on the unlit cigar — the cold draw — testing the resistance and tasting the raw leaf.
rites.why: The cold draw is the only preview the fire allows. It confirms the draw is right and gives the first honest taste of the blend.

rites.name: The cut
rites.how: Choose the instrument: the guillotine takes the whole face, the V-cut a clean wedge, the punch a small round opening. Whatever the tool, cut above the line of the cap — at the shoulder, never below it.
rites.why: The cap is the only thing anchoring the wrapper to the head. Cut below its line and the cigar can unravel in your hand.

rites.name: Toasting the foot
rites.how: Hold the foot near the flame without letting it touch, rotating until the rim glows evenly. Only then bring the cigar to your lips and draw the fire home.
rites.why: An even start is an even burn. A cigar rushed into flame chars one side and runs, and the first minutes are spent correcting instead of tasting.

rites.name: Never inhale
rites.how: Draw the smoke into the mouth, let it rest on the palate, and release it. Experienced tasters sometimes push a little out through the nose — the retrohale — to read the aroma.
rites.why: Cigar smoke is not meant for the lungs. The palate and the nose are the instruments; everything the blender composed is legible there.

rites.name: The ash
rites.how: Let the ash build to an inch or so, then roll or tap it gently into the tray before it falls on its own. A cigar is never flicked like a cigarette.
rites.why: A firm, long ash is the signature of well-rolled long filler. Tradition holds that it also shields the coal and keeps the burn cool — lore, but lore that generations of tasters keep repeating.

rites.name: The band question
rites.how: Leave the band on until the cigar has warmed well into its smoking; then, if you choose to remove it, slide it off gently. If it resists, leave it be.
rites.why: The etiquette — old custom read a displayed band as boasting — is tradition, not law. The practical part is real: heat softens the band's gum, and a warm band comes away without tearing the wrapper.

rites.name: The three thirds
rites.how: Read the cigar in thirds: the first introduces the blend, the second develops it, and the final third is the strongest and darkest.
rites.why: Blenders compose cigars to evolve, and the smoke drawn through the remaining leaf carries flavor and strength forward as it shortens. The end of a cigar is always more concentrated than its beginning.

rites.name: The resting pace
rites.how: Set the cigar down in the tray between draws and let it wait — about a minute is the customary rhythm.
rites.why: Drawing too often overheats the coal, and a hot cigar turns bitter. Rested, it stays cool and keeps telling the truth.

rites.name: The dignified end
rites.how: When you are finished, do not stub or crush the cigar. Lay it in the ashtray and let it go out on its own.
rites.why: Left alone, a cigar dies quietly within a few minutes; ground out, it releases its harshest smoke. Tradition adds that a thing which took years to make has earned an unhurried end.

rites.name: The relight
rites.how: A cigar that has gone out may be relit within a few hours without shame. First purge it — blow gently outward through the cigar to expel the stale smoke — then knock off the loose ash and toast the foot as if for the first time.
rites.why: Stale smoke and tars gather at a dead coal. The purge and a fresh toast recover most of what the cigar was; leave it until tomorrow and less of it will answer.

aromas.essence: A cigar's aroma is the record of everything that happened to the leaf — the soil it drank, the heat it survived, the cedar it slept beside. The spectrum runs from fresh hay to dark espresso.

families.source: Terroir and deep fermentation — the leaf remembering its ground; strongest in Cuban and Nicaraguan filler.
Years spent in cedar-lined aging rooms and cedar boxes; the wood breathes into the leaf.
Ligero — the sun-hardened top primings — and volcanic soils, Estelí's above all.
The leaf's natural sugars, concentrated by the long, hot fermentations that make a maduro.
Shade-grown Connecticut-seed wrappers and gentle seco leaf — mildness with texture.
Extended aging of filler leaf; the smell of time itself doing its work.
Dark, thick wrappers — San Andrés and Connecticut Broadleaf maduro — whose hot fermentation creates roast-like depths.
Young leaf, pale claro wrappers, and the flash-cured green of candela — the bright end of the spectrum.

techniques.name: Entubado bunching
techniques.what: Each filler leaf is rolled into its own slender tube before the tubes are gathered into the bunch — the slowest, most exacting way to build a cigar's interior.
techniques.effect: Open, even airflow through every leaf: the best draw a cigar can have, and the fullest expression of the blend.

techniques.name: Book and accordion bunching
techniques.what: Filler leaves are laid flat and folded like the pages of a book, or with edges pleated inward accordion-style, then rolled into the binder.
techniques.effect: Faster than entubado and reliable in skilled hands; the accordion fold preserves air channels that plain folding can crush.

techniques.name: The triple cap
techniques.what: The head of the cigar is finished with three overlapping turns of cap leaf — the classic Cuban signature, visible as three fine seams.
techniques.effect: The head survives cutting cleanly, and the wrapper stays anchored to the last inch.

techniques.name: Box-pressing
techniques.what: Cigars are pressed square-shouldered, a shape born when Cuban cigars were packed tightly in trunks and kept it as a virtue.
techniques.effect: A softer feel in the hand, a slightly opened draw, and a slower, cooler burn along the flattened sides.

techniques.name: Shade growing (tapado)
techniques.what: Wrapper plants are raised under vast cloth tents that soften the sun.
techniques.effect: Thin, elastic, fine-veined leaves of even color — the silk of the cigar world.

techniques.name: Sun growing
techniques.what: Plants stand in full, unfiltered sun.
techniques.effect: Thicker leaves, heavier oils, more sugar and strength — the raw material of filler, and of dark, sweet maduro wrappers.

techniques.name: Priming by position
techniques.what: Leaves are harvested by their height on the stalk, a few at a time, over successive passes: volado at the bottom, seco in the middle, ligero at the crown.
techniques.effect: Each priming is a distinct ingredient — burn, aroma, power — kept separate from field to blending bench.

techniques.name: Blending ligero, seco, and volado
techniques.what: The blender composes the filler: ligero for strength at the core, seco for aroma around it, volado to carry the burn.
techniques.effect: Balance. A cigar of pure ligero would barely stay lit and would flatten the smoker; the blend makes power drinkable.

techniques.name: Aging in Spanish cedar
techniques.what: Leaf, and later finished cigars, rest in rooms and boxes lined with Spanish cedar, the cigar's traditional companion wood.
techniques.effect: Cedar breathes with the humidity, discourages the tobacco beetle, and lends the quiet woody note smokers know before the first light.

techniques.name: Candela flash-curing
techniques.what: Wrapper leaf is heat-cured in a matter of days instead of weeks, locking the chlorophyll before it can fade.
techniques.effect: A green wrapper with a light, grassy, faintly sweet taste — the brightest, strangest color a cigar can wear.

vitolas.name: Petit Corona
vitolas.note: The short classic — a complete Cuban statement in about half an hour.

vitolas.name: Corona
vitolas.note: The historical yardstick of the habano; every other size is described by how it departs from this one.

vitolas.name: Corona Gorda
vitolas.note: A corona with broader shoulders — more filler, more volume of smoke, the same measured pace.

vitolas.name: Robusto
vitolas.note: Short, thick, and generous — the modern favorite; roughly 45 minutes of full flavor.

vitolas.name: Toro
vitolas.note: The new world's workhorse — a robusto given room to develop its argument.

vitolas.name: Churchill
vitolas.note: Named for the man who smoked Romeo y Julieta by the thousand; a long, stately evening of a cigar.

vitolas.name: Double Corona
vitolas.note: The grand format — nearly two hours, and a blend with time enough to change its mind twice.

vitolas.name: Torpedo / Pirámide
vitolas.note: A tapered head that concentrates the smoke; the cut decides the draw, so cut with intention.

vitolas.name: Lancero
vitolas.note: Long and slender — the wrapper dominates the blend, so only confident wrapper leaf dares this shape.

vitolas.name: Perfecto
vitolas.note: Closed at both ends and swelling in the middle; dimensions vary by maker — a shape from the cigar's ornate past, kept alive by rollers who like a challenge.

wrappers.name: Candela
wrappers.flavor: Grassy, light, faintly sweet — chlorophyll locked in by flash heat-curing.

wrappers.name: Claro
wrappers.flavor: Delicate and neutral, often shade-grown; it lets the filler speak first.

wrappers.name: Colorado Claro
wrappers.flavor: Dry, subtle sweetness with a soft woody note — the classic 'natural' wrapper.

wrappers.name: Colorado
wrappers.flavor: Aromatic and balanced — the middle of the spectrum, where fragrance peaks.

wrappers.name: Colorado Maduro
wrappers.flavor: Richer and rounder, leaning toward the dark end without its full weight.

wrappers.name: Maduro
wrappers.flavor: Cocoa, coffee, and natural sweetness — the reward of longer, hotter fermentation.

wrappers.name: Oscuro
wrappers.flavor: Earthy, dense, and dark-sweet — top-priming leaf fermented longest of all.
